newsitem.title: UK: Chronology of Britain's political ties with Europe.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Britain's political ties with Europe.

text.p: Following is a chronology of Britain's political ties with Europe since the 1950s.
1951 - Germany and France pilot treaty establishing European Coal and Steel Community. Britain, worried by supra-nationalist implications, does not join.
1958 - European Economic Community established by Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands and Luxembourg after Britain's idea for a free trade area within Europe was rejected.
1960 - Britain forms European Free Trade Association (EFTA) with six other European countries outside EEC.
1961 - Conservative government applies to join EEC but warns it would hurt ties with its Commonwealth countries (colonies and former colonies).
1963 - French President Charles De Gaulle vetoes application.
1967 - Labour government announces its intention to join EEC, but idea again vetoed by de Gaulle.

1971 - Conservative government says it plans to enter EEC. Bill takes five months to clear parliament. Labour call for a referendum, defeated in parliament, leads to resignation of deputy leader Roy Jenkins.
1972 - Britain forced to leave the European currency "snake", forerunner of Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) after just six weeks.
1973 - Britain enters EEC.
1974 - Labour wins election; pledges during campaign it would hold referendum on whether Britain should remain in EEC
1975 - Government recommends "yes" vote in referendum, first to involve whole of Britain. "Yes" wins 67.2 percent of vote, "no" 32.8 percent.

1979 - Election of Conservative government under Margaret Thatcher. At November summit, she precipitates first of many crises at heads of government meetings during 1980s by demanding reduction in Britain's net contribution to EEC.
EEC agrees rebates for Britain in 1980, 1981 and 1982.
1983 - Summit dissolves in disagreement over Thatcher's demands for further rebate. Eventually, permanent formula on rebate worked out after EEC withholds refunds to Britain.
1985 - Britain agrees to sign the Single European Act, to establish a common trading market in EEC from 1992.
Thatcher becomes increasingly concerned about move towards federalism in community and monetary integration which she felt would diminish British sovereignity.
1988 - Thatcher gives speech at Bruges, Belgium, where she outlines her concerns about future direction of EEC.
1990, October - Sterling joins ERM as finance minister John Major persuades Thatcher to end her opposition. At Rome summit, Thatcher resists move towards single European currency.
November - Thatcher resigns as Conservative party leader, partly because of attacks on her dealings with Europe.
1991, December - Britain signs the Maastricht Treaty on political and monetary union but wins opt-outs on social chapter, covering workers' rights, and monetary union.
1992, September - Sterling forced out of ERM after Britain spent billions of pounds of reserves supporting it.
November - Government narrowly wins parliamentary vote on Maastricht treaty.
1993, July - Major calls, and wins, vote of confidence on European policy after 23 Eurosceptic Conservatives vote against government in key vote on Maastricht treaty ratification.
1995, July - Major defeats right-wing Eurosceptic challenger John Redwood in election for party leadership.
1996, March - Mad cow crisis erupts after Britain announces possible link between eating beef and fatal brain disease CJD. EU slaps export ban on British beef.
Start of Inter-Governmental Conference to review Maastricht Treaty. Britain began negotiations isolated on many issues and remains so.

May - Major says he will obstruct normal EU business until beef ban is lifted. This non-cooperation is halted by agreement at June summit to lift ban gradually in return for measures to eradicate mad cow disease.
